common_name: Kanpyo Gourd (Japanese Dried Gourd Strip Bottle Gourd)

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early in short-season regions; give the vigorous vine a strong arbor or wide bed to sprawl since fruit is harvested well before the shell hardens.

directions: Kanpyo is the Japanese bottle gourd cultivar grown specifically to be peeled into long ribbons and sun-dried into the sweet-savory strips used in kanpyomaki sushi rolls and simmered dishes, distinct from gourds grown for eating fresh or for hard dried shells. Vines are vigorous and need a sturdy trellis or wide open ground, with large white flowers opening at dusk for moth pollination, so hand-pollinating with a small brush in the evening improves fruit set where night pollinators are scarce. Harvest the pale green fruit while still immature and tender, before the seeds and rind harden, then peel it in one continuous spiral ribbon with a vegetable peeler or specialized gourd slicer and hang the strips to dry in a warm, airy spot out of direct sun. Because the plant is a heavy, sprawling grower that benefits from consistent warmth and moisture through fruit development, it performs best where summers are long and hot.
sources: Purdue University — New Crop Resources — Lagenaria siceraria

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed once soil is reliably warm; kakri is a fast, heat-loving South Asian vegetable melon that grows quickly through hot summer weather and bears over a long harvest window if picked young and often.

directions: Kakri is a slender, pale green to lightly mottled melon grown throughout North India and Pakistan not for sweetness but as a fresh vegetable, eaten raw in salads, juiced, or cooked in curries much like cucumber. Give the sprawling vine a trellis or let it run along the ground, keeping soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit set since irregular watering toughens the skin and turns the flesh bitter. Harvest fruit young and slender, typically 8 to 12 inches long, well before the interior seeds mature and the rind coarsens, and pick every few days to keep the vine setting new fruit rather than ripening old ones to full size. It thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that stress many true cucumbers, making it a reliable substitute crop for gardeners in punishing summer heat.
sources: Purdue University — New Crop Resources — Cucumis melo var. utilissimus

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early in short-season regions; provide a trellis or arbor so the club-shaped fruit hangs straight and stays clean.

directions: Opo, also called upo in the Philippines and known across Southeast and East Asian cuisines as a mild, absorbent summer vegetable, is a shorter, plumper, club-shaped bottle gourd cultivar harvested young and tender rather than left to mature and dry like ornamental or dipper-type gourds. Train the sprawling vine onto a trellis or overhead arbor so fruit hangs straight instead of curling on the ground, and hand-pollinate at dusk with a soft brush where moth activity is low, since the large white flowers open only in the evening. Harvest fruit at 10 to 14 inches long while the skin is still glossy and easily pierced with a fingernail; overmature fruit develops a tough rind and spongy, seedy flesh unsuitable for cooking. Peeled and sliced, the mild flesh readily takes on the flavor of broths, stir-fries, and sautés, making it a staple in Filipino sinigang and ginisang upo as well as Vietnamese and Chinese home cooking.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

common_name: Sugar Kiss Melon (AAS-Winning High-Sugar Hybrid Cantaloupe)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s; Sugar Kiss sets fruit reliably over a compact vine, making it a good fit for smaller vegetable gardens.

directions: Sugar Kiss is a modern hybrid cantaloupe bred by Sakata Seed and recognized with an All-America Selections award for combining exceptionally high sugar content with a compact, manageable vine that suits smaller home gardens better than traditional sprawling cantaloupe types. Fruits are heavily netted, medium-sized, and ripen with a strong sweet aroma at the blossom end, developing flesh that consistently tests sweeter on the brix scale than many older open-pollinated cantaloupe varieties. Sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost and keep moisture consistent through flowering and fruit set, then ease back on watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with gentle pressure and the netted rind has taken on a golden cast beneath the netting.
sources: All-America Selections — Sugar Kiss melon variety notes
Sakata Seed America — Sugar Kiss cantaloupe

common_name: Da Vinci Melon (Sweet Disease-Resistant Galia-Type Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed once soil is thoroughly warm; Da Vinci is a vigorous, disease-tolerant vine that rewards consistent moisture through fruit set and a drier finish as melons ripen.

directions: Da Vinci is a Galia-type hybrid melon bred by Rijk Zwaan that has become a favorite among home gardeners and market growers for pairing intensely sweet, aromatic green-to-orange flesh with strong resistance to powdery mildew, a disease that often cuts melon harvests short in humid climates. The round, lightly netted fruit ripens with the fragrant, floral perfume characteristic of Galia and Charentais-type melons rather than the heavier musk of standard American cantaloupe. Give the vigorous vine full sun and generously amended, well-drained soil, keeping moisture even through flowering and fruit development before tapering off as the fruit nears harvest to concentrate sugars. Judge ripeness by a shift in background color toward gold beneath the netting, a strong sweet aroma at the blossom end, and a clean slip from the vine with light pressure.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Da Vinci melon variety notes
Renee's Garden Seeds — Da Vinci melon

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; Lambkin's early maturity and compact habit make it well suited to shorter-season gardens and large containers.

directions: Lambkin is a Burpee-introduced, All-America Selections-winning melon bred to bring French Charentais-style eating quality to a compact vine and an early, personal-size fruit about the size of a small cantaloupe. The smooth, lightly ribbed gray-green rind encloses deep orange, richly perfumed flesh with the concentrated sweetness and floral aroma typical of Charentais types, but on a plant far more manageable than the long-vining French heirlooms it descends from. Grow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping moisture steady through fruit set and easing off as the small melons approach ripeness to intensify their sugars. Because Charentais-type melons slip cleanly from the vine only at full ripeness, check plants daily near the expected harvest window and watch for a softening and light cracking at the stem end as the surest sign of peak flavor.
sources: All-America Selections — Lambkin melon variety notes
